newsitem.title: CONGO: Hydro-power helps Congo cut electricity imports.
newsitem.headline: Hydro-power helps Congo cut electricity imports.

text.p: Oil producer Congo, striving to inject new life into its listless economy, is part way through an ambitious programme to boost domestic electricity generation and it has already started to feel the benefit.
But with work having begun on a huge project at Sounda in Kouilou region in the west, officials say it is hoping one day to become an exporter of power to neighbours on the world's poorest continent.
Officials at the state power company Societe Nationale d'Electricite (SNE) say that electricity imports from Zaire dropped from 45 percent of needs in 1995 to two percent in 1996.
This follows the rehabilitation in May of the Djoue River hydro-electric plant with the help of South African funding and expertise, they add.

Congo, despite its oil exports, slipped into economic decline in the 1980s but the government of President Pascal Lissouba is working to cut its budget deficit under the guidance of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.
Officials say that Congo has run up a debt estimated at nine billion CFA francs with neighbouring Zaire for electricity imports from its giant Inga dam.
Self-sufficiency in power generation is a goal several other pre-emerging African economies -- notably Ivory Coast and Ghana -- have set themselves.
Congo, like Zaire, has considerable hydro-electric potential on the rivers that criss-cross its territory. A tiny part of its generating capacity is thermal.
Djoue, outside the capital Brazzaville, is the oldest hydro-electric plant in Central Africa. The 15-megawatt plant was knocked out of action by a flood in 1991.
South African company Rotek provided the expertise to get it working again while the South African Investek Bank Limited provided the funding in the form of a 4.5 billion CFA loan.
Officials say the annual saving of bringing Djoue back on stream will be an estimated 800 million CFA francs.

The government launched a two-year programme in 1995 to cut Congo's dependence on Zairean electricity, to extend electricity to more homes and above all to ensure that the national economy enjoys what it dubbed high quality and adequate energy supply.
Congo's main plant -- 74 MW -- is on the Bouenza River.
The Djoue scheme was just one of several designed to boost Congo's electricity production capacity from 162 megawatts to 412 megawatts using plants powered by the nation's rivers.

The programme requires investment of 206 billion CFA francs 79 percent of which the government hopes to fund from the private sector, 18.5 percent from its own resources and 2.5 percent from the state power company. It has high hopes of encouraging further South African investment.
The largest project, launched on June 15 by Lissouba, envisages construction of a 1,000 megawatt dam at Sounda in the Kouilou region. Work is expected to take at least 18 months.
Other projects include construction of 11 small hydro-electric plants and 110 km (70 miles) of power lines.
Lissouba won a presidential election in 1992 during Congo's turbulent democratic transition.

Congo signed a three-year programme with the IMF in June. The Paris Club of official creditors agreed in July to write off two-thirds of the Central African country's external debt, which now stands at about $1.2 billion.
($1=512 CFA francs)
